findings.message: `waitUntil` is a plain (non-suspend) function that advances the `TestCoroutineScheduler` in a tight loop. When called from inside a `runTest(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))` body the calling coroutine is never suspended, so any tasks that `advanceTimeBy` enqueues onto `StandardTestDispatcher` will not run until after `waitUntil` returns and the test coroutine yields. The function works today only because every condition it checks is driven by `UnconfinedTestDispatcher`-dispatched callbacks. Any future test whose condition depends on a coroutine launched in the `runTest` body (on `StandardTestDispatcher`) will silently exhaust all 500 iterations and throw a misleading time-out error rather than actually waiting for the work to complete.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Each `advanceTimeBy` triggers pending coroutines; condition becomes true early
findings.severity_justification: All current 14 `waitUntil` call-sites check conditions driven by `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` callbacks and work correctly. The risk is forward-looking: a future test author who adds a `waitUntil` condition driven by a `StandardTestDispatcher` coroutine will get a misleading 5s-virtual-time error instead of the real diagnosis.
findings.category_justification: The issue is in a test helper that shapes how future component tests can be written; incorrect use would cause silent test failures.

findings.message: `tearDown()` calls `runBlocking { it.close(); it.done.await() }` with no timeout. `close()` internally calls `scope.coroutineContext[Job]?.cancelAndJoin()` and only completes `_done` inside `shutdown()` afterwards. If any child coroutine of the client scope fails to respond to cancellation (e.g. a spin loop or an uncancellable blocking call inside a production code path), `done` will never complete and `tearDown` will block the JUnit test thread indefinitely. JUnit 5 has no built-in timeout for `@AfterEach`, so a single such test will stall the entire suite with no recovery path.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The claim is factually correct: `runBlocking` in `tearDown()` has no timeout guard, and `close()` blocks on `cancelAndJoin()` before completing `_done`, so an uncancellable coroutine would stall the entire test suite. However, the identical pattern existed in all 5 classes before this PR; the change only centralizes it.
findings.severity_justification: All production coroutines use cancellable patterns (delay, channel iteration, CancellationException handling), so a real hang is unlikely. The concern is theoretical and pre-existing, not a regression introduced here.
findings.category_justification: The issue is about test harness resilience — a lack of timeout guard in teardown that could stall the CI suite if production code misbehaved.

findings.message: All `CompletableDeferred.await()` calls (throughout `BasicTest`, `CallbackTest`, `LifecycleTest`, `ReconnectTest`) lost their explicit time bounds when `CountDownLatch.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` was replaced. The old latches failed the test with a clear assertion after 5 real seconds. Now, if a callback never fires due to a regression, the `await()` suspends inside `runTest` until its 60-second real-time deadline, making CI wait 60 s per failing case rather than 5 s. Given that the safety argument ('the deferred is always completed before await() is reached') holds only under the current `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` behaviour, any dispatcher change silently turns bounded tests into slow-hanging ones.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Factually correct: the old `CountDownLatch.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` provided explicit 5-second bounds; the new `CompletableDeferred.await()` has no per-call timeout and defers to `runTest`'s 60-second real-time ceiling. The current safety argument (UnconfinedTestDispatcher makes callbacks synchronous before `await()` is reached) holds today but the finding correctly identifies that any deviation silently increases per-failing-test CI wait from 5s to 60s.
findings.severity_justification: No current test is broken; the concern is about slower CI feedback for future regressions. The 60s runTest timeout still bounds test duration — it's a diagnostic quality issue, not a correctness issue.
findings.category_justification: The issue is about test failure observability and CI speed — explicit time bounds being removed from assertions during test migration.

findings.message: In `throwing onTransportDrop in reconnect loop does not abort reconnect`, `transport3.autoPong()` is called but its return value (the `PongResponder`) is immediately discarded. `PongResponder.tick()` is never called for transport3, so no pong is ever injected after the ping. The test ends by asserting only that a ping was sent to transport3 (`waitForPing(transport3)`), but the pong handshake is never completed. The pong-deadline timer starts counting from the moment the ping is sent; teardown cancels the scope before 60 s of virtual time, so no timeout fires in practice — but the test never verifies that the third reconnect established a healthy, pong-acknowledged connection.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Factually correct: `transport3.autoPong()` return value is discarded and `tick()` is never called, so no pong is injected and the pong handshake for transport3 is never completed. The pong-deadline timer does start counting. However this exact pattern existed in the pre-PR code — the PR did not introduce it.
findings.severity_justification: The test's primary assertion (reconnect loop doesn't abort despite a throwing callback) is correctly verified. The missing pong tick for transport3 is a test-completeness gap, not a correctness bug — teardown cancels the scope harmlessly before the 60s virtual deadline would fire.
findings.category_justification: The issue is about incomplete test verification — a secondary assertion (pong handshake completing) is absent from the test.

findings.message: In `handles server rejection gracefully`, `testClient = client` is placed inside the try block after `WspulseClient.connectInternal()`. Because `connectInternal` is expected to throw, that assignment is never reached and `testClient` remains `null` — teardown is a no-op. If a future regression makes `connectInternal` succeed instead of throwing, `fail()` raises `AssertionError` (which extends `Error`, not `Exception`, so it bypasses the `catch` block), but `testClient` was already assigned. Teardown then closes the client, which silently hides the leaked-resource scenario. The try/catch should be structured so that a client that unexpectedly succeeds is always tracked in `testClient` before any assertion fires.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding's conclusion is wrong. In the regression case (connectInternal unexpectedly succeeds), `testClient = client` IS executed before `fail()` fires, so the client IS tracked and teardown WILL close it. The finding says 'the try/catch should be structured so that a client that unexpectedly succeeds is always tracked in testClient before any assertion fires' — but the current code already does exactly that. In the normal (throw) case, `connectInternal` internally cleans up before rethrowing, so there is no resource leak regardless.
findings.severity_justification: The finding describes a non-existent problem; the code already handles both scenarios correctly.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns test resource management and try/catch structure in a test method.

findings.message: In `close during reconnect fires onDisconnect null`, after `client.close()` the test asserts `assertTrue(disconnectCalled.isCompleted)` synchronously (no `await()`). This is correct only because `close()` calls `shutdown()` synchronously after `cancelAndJoin()`, and `shutdown()` calls `onDisconnect` before completing `_done`. This execution order is an implementation detail of `WspulseClient.close()`. If `shutdown()` is ever made asynchronous (e.g. dispatched via `scope.launch`) the assertion will silently pass a non-completed deferred, turning a real bug into a false green. The safer pattern used elsewhere is `assertTrue(disconnectCalled.isCompleted)` only after `client.done.await()`.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding's core claim is factually incorrect. If `disconnectCalled` were not completed when `assertTrue(disconnectCalled.isCompleted)` runs, `assertTrue(false)` would throw AssertionError and fail the test — a correct failure detection, not a false green. The finding has the logic backwards: the `isCompleted` check fails faster than `await()` would. The current code is correct and the failure scenario described does not produce a false green.
findings.severity_justification: The finding describes a non-existent failure mode; the test correctly detects the scenario it's supposed to detect.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about test assertion robustness and failure detection semantics.

findings.message: The `waitUntil` call does not advance virtual time via `testScheduler.runCurrent()` after the loop. This can lead to flaky tests if the `received.size` check depends on coroutines that have been dispatched but not yet executed by the `UnconfinedTestDispatcher`. Since `injectText` triggers `onMessage` which runs in a coroutine on the client's scope, there's a possibility that `waitUntil` exits before all `onMessage` callbacks have completed, making the final assertion on `received.size` unreliable. Adding `testScheduler.runCurrent()` after the `waitUntil` call ensures all pending tasks on the scheduler are executed before proceeding.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding misunderstands UnconfinedTestDispatcher behavior. When `injectText` calls `trySend`, the suspended `readLoop` is resumed immediately in the current thread (eager dispatch). All `onMessage` callbacks complete synchronously within each `injectText` call. By the time the injection loop finishes and `waitUntil` is evaluated, `received.size` already equals `total`. There is no 'dispatched but not yet executed' window with UnconfinedTestDispatcher.
findings.severity_justification: The described race condition does not exist under UnconfinedTestDispatcher; the test is correct as written.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about test reliability and execution ordering of callback invocations.

findings.message: The `waitForPing` call is not followed by `testScheduler.runCurrent()`. This may cause flakiness because `waitForPing` advances time but does not guarantee that coroutines scheduled to run at that virtual time (like the `pingLoop` in `WspulseClient`) have actually executed. The subsequent call to `pongResponder.tick()` might run before the ping is processed, leading to unpredictable test behavior. Adding `testScheduler.runCurrent()` after `waitForPing` will ensure the ping-related coroutine has executed before the test proceeds.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The line reference is wrong (line 91 is a `waitUntil` call, not `waitForPing`). On substance: `pingLoop` sends its initial ping eagerly with `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` before `waitForPing` is called, so `waitForPing` takes the fast path without advancing time. Even when `advanceTimeBy` is used, it runs pending tasks synchronously per `TestCoroutineScheduler` semantics. `waitForPing` only returns when the ping IS in `transport.sent`, so `pongResponder.tick()` is always called after the ping is confirmed present.
findings.severity_justification: The described race condition does not exist; the initial ping fires eagerly with UnconfinedTestDispatcher and waitForPing provides a positive confirmation before proceeding.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about test execution ordering and potential flakiness in test infrastructure.

findings.message: The `tearDown` method uses `runBlocking(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler))`. While `runBlocking` is necessary here because `@AfterEach` cannot be a suspend function, using `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` can lead to unpredictable behavior. It executes tasks eagerly, which might not be what's expected if there are other coroutines interacting with the client during teardown. A safer approach would be to use a `StandardTestDispatcher` and explicitly run pending tasks with `testScheduler.runCurrent()` to ensure a predictable execution order.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The `UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)` choice was deliberate and documented in commit 5a2dc4b: plain `runBlocking` caused deadlocks when a test failed mid-way because nothing drained the test scheduler. The recommended alternative (StandardTestDispatcher + runCurrent()) is impractical inside `runBlocking` since you cannot call `runCurrent()` from the blocked thread while waiting for `close()` to complete. The finding's concern is generic and speculative with no concrete failure scenario.
findings.severity_justification: The finding's recommendation would degrade teardown reliability rather than improve it; the existing choice is deliberately correct.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about test teardown dispatcher choice and execution order.

findings.message: The assertion `assertTrue(disconnectCalled.isCompleted)` is used instead of `disconnectCalled.await()`. While this works because `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` runs the disconnection logic synchronously, it makes the test more brittle. It relies on the implementation detail of the dispatcher. Using `await()` would be more idiomatic and robust, as it correctly suspends until the deferred is complete, regardless of the dispatcher's behavior. The test timeout would handle cases where it never completes.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding has the robustness argument backwards. `assertTrue(disconnectCalled.isCompleted)` fails immediately with a clear AssertionError if the callback didn't fire; `await()` would hang for 60s before timing out. The test already explicitly drains the scheduler via `advanceTimeBy(350)` + `runCurrent()` before checking — so `isCompleted` asserts a timing property (fired during the scheduler drain), which is stronger than `await()`. The 'brittle' characterization is incorrect.
findings.severity_justification: The current pattern is intentionally stricter than await(); swapping to await() would be a correctness downgrade, not an improvement.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about test assertion style and coroutine idioms.

findings.message: The assertion `assertTrue(transportRestored.isCompleted)` is used instead of `transportRestored.await()`. This relies on the `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` executing the callback that completes the deferred synchronously. A more robust and idiomatic approach in coroutine testing is to use `await()` to suspend until the action is complete, which works correctly with any test dispatcher. The overall test timeout will prevent the test from hanging if the deferred is never completed.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Same pattern as findings 6 and 10: `assertTrue(isCompleted)` after explicitly draining the scheduler is stricter than `await()`, failing immediately with AssertionError rather than hanging 60s. The test explicitly calls `advanceTimeBy` + `runCurrent()` before checking, so `isCompleted` asserts a timing property about when the callback fired. The finding mischaracterizes the faster-failing pattern as 'brittle' and the slower-failing one as 'robust'.
findings.severity_justification: The current pattern is correct and intentionally stricter; the suggested change would weaken the test's timing assertions.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about test assertion style in coroutine virtual-time tests.

findings.message: The assertion `assertTrue(disconnectCalled.isCompleted)` is used instead of `disconnectCalled.await()`. While this works with an `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` because the disconnection logic runs synchronously within the test thread, it is less robust than using `await()`. Using `await()` is the idiomatic way to wait for a `CompletableDeferred` and ensures the test works correctly even if the dispatcher implementation changes. The test would rely on the `runTest` timeout to fail if the deferred never completes.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Identical pattern to findings 6, 10, and 11. `assertTrue(disconnectCalled.isCompleted)` after `advanceTimeBy` + `runCurrent()` is intentionally strict — it fails immediately if the callback didn't fire during the scheduler drain, whereas `await()` would hang 60s before timing out. The finding's 'more robust' characterization of await() is backwards.
findings.severity_justification: The current pattern is correct and stricter than await(); no actual robustness issue exists.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about test assertion style in virtual-time coroutine tests.

findings.message: The `disconnectCalled` CompletableDeferred is awaited, but if it is never completed due to an issue in configuring the client callbacks or the testing infrastructure, the test will hang indefinitely. Consider adding timeout handling like withTimeout.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is generic boilerplate — 'any await() without timeout could hang' — without accounting for the specific ordering. Both `transportDropFired` and `disconnectCalled` are completed synchronously inside `close()` → `shutdown()` → callbacks, all of which complete before `client.done.await()` returns. The subsequent `await()` calls are no-ops. The finding could be copy-pasted verbatim onto any coroutine test with an `await()` call.
findings.severity_justification: The specific `await()` calls are already guaranteed to be complete by the time they're reached; adding `withTimeout` would be misleading noise.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about test robustness and potential hanging in test infrastructure.

findings.message: `waitUntil` never re-checks the condition after the final virtual-time advance. If the condition becomes true during the last 10 ms slice (or at the 5 s boundary), the helper still throws even though it was satisfied within the documented 5 s window. Add a final condition check after the loop (and run currently due tasks if needed) before failing.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The loop checks the condition before each advance but never after the final (500th) advance. A condition satisfied at exactly 5000ms virtual time would cause a false error throw. This is verifiable by reading the repeat loop structure in the new ComponentTestBase.kt.
findings.severity_justification: Only affects test infrastructure, not production code. With UnconfinedTestDispatcher dispatching synchronously, conditions are practically always satisfied early in the loop. A spurious failure at the exact 5s boundary is unlikely but real.
findings.category_justification: It's a logic error in the loop termination check — the condition is not evaluated after the last virtual-time advance, so the function can throw when the condition was actually satisfied within the documented window.

findings.message: `waitForPing` is the same kind of subclass helper as `clientConfig` and `waitUntil`, but it is declared `internal` while the other helpers are `protected`. Since searches only show subclass usages, this unnecessarily exposes the helper to the whole test module; make it `protected` unless broader module-level access is intentional.
findings.tp_fp_justification: `MockTransport` is internal; Kotlin forbids protected members exposing internal types
findings.severity_justification: This is a visibility inconsistency in test-only code with no behavioral impact. It unnecessarily widens the API surface of the helper within the module but causes no bugs.
findings.category_justification: It's a naming/visibility inconsistency between related members of the same class — a code style/convention issue with no runtime impact.
